During the 1920s, the United States experienced technological changes in the workplace that allowed more goods to be produced. These goods were then sold both within the United States and all over the world, especially in Europe. Over time, more goods were produced than people had the money or desire to pay for, which is called
. Overproduction led to lower prices for goods, less profit for companies, and lower wages for workers.

contents.text: By 1929, overproduction contributed to the economic recession that would become the Great Depression. Match the changes to the way they led to overproduction.

draggableItems.text: Workers became specialized at their tasks, which allowed for more goods to be produced much more quickly at lower costs.
Factories could run both day and night, so companies produced more goods.
Machines became easier to assemble and repair, which reduced costs and encouraged companies to maximize their output.

staticItems.text: The parts used to run factory machines were standardized across industries, which made them easy to acquire.
Assembly lines in factories broke down workers' tasks into simple actions that were easy to repeat.
The adoption of electricity provided factories with lighting and more reliable machines powered by the electric grid.

explanationText.text: The advertisement says that people could pay off their cars in monthly installments rather than all at once. When people lost their jobs at the beginning of the Great Depression, they were unable to continue paying back these loans, leaving many in debt.

explanationText.text: The advertisement shows a car driving in winter, but this did not contribute to economic hardship during the Great Depression.

contents.text: While new consumer goods raised the standard of living for many people, the farm economy in the United States struggled throughout the 1920s. As with other industries, mechanization and technological changes led to overproduction of food and low crop prices. The consequences of these developments contributed to the start of the Great Depression and made life worse during it.
Match each development in agriculture with its most immediate consequence.

draggableItems.text: When profits declined, farmers couldn't repay banks, which caused the banks to repossess farms and farmers to lose their livelihood.
Because their costs to produce food remained high, producing too many crops at a low price destroyed farmers' profits.
Overuse of the land weakened the soil's structure, making it especially vulnerable to droughts.

staticItems.text: During World War I, farmers increased their production to meet high demand for food, but they continued this production even when demand fell after the war.
Both during and after World War I, farmers borrowed money from banks to expand operations and to sustain their businesses.
To boost short-term production, farmers relied on intensive farming techniques, like deep plowing, which removed nutrients from the soil.

contents.text: While new consumer goods raised the standard of living for many people, the farm economy in the United States struggled throughout the 1920s. As with other industries, mechanization and technological changes led to overproduction of food and low crop prices. The consequences of these developments contributed to the start of the Great Depression and made life worse during it.
Match each problem of overproduction with the agricultural development that led to it.

draggableItems.text: Both during and after World War I, farmers borrowed money from banks to expand operations and to sustain their businesses.
During World War I, farmers increased their production to meet high demand for food, but they continued this production even when demand fell after the war.
To boost short-term production, farmers relied on intensive farming techniques, like deep plowing, which removed nutrients from the soil.

staticItems.text: Because their costs to produce food remained high, producing too many crops at a low price destroyed farmers' profits.
When profits declined, farmers couldn't repay banks, which caused the banks to repossess farms and farmers to lose their livelihood.
Overuse of the land weakened the soil's structure, making it especially vulnerable to droughts.

During the 1920s, the United States experienced technological changes in the workplace that allowed more goods to be produced. These goods were then sold both within the United States and all over the world, especially in Europe. Over time, more goods were produced than people had the money or desire to pay for, which is called
. Overproduction led to lower prices for goods, less profit for companies, and lower wages for workers.

contents.text: By 1929, overproduction contributed to the economic recession that would become the Great Depression. Match the changes to the way they led to overproduction.

draggableItems.text: Workers became specialized at their tasks, which allowed for more goods to be produced much more quickly at lower costs.
Factories could run both day and night, so companies produced more goods.
Machines became easier to assemble and repair, which reduced costs and encouraged companies to maximize their output.

staticItems.text: The parts used to run factory machines were standardized across industries, which made them easy to acquire.
The adoption of electricity provided factories with lighting and more reliable machines powered by the electric grid.
Assembly lines in factories broke down workers' tasks into simple actions that were easy to repeat.

. Overproduction led to lower prices for goods, less profit for companies, and lower wages for workers.

contents.text: When the Great Depression began in 1929, Americans looked to President Herbert Hoover for leadership. Hoover's response was shaped by his beliefs that the downturn was temporary and that the government should avoid intervening in the economy. He urged businesses to avoid cutting jobs, and he encouraged Americans to rely on local charity rather than federal assistance.
Look at the images and read the captions related to public opinion of Hoover during the Great Depression. Then answer the question below.

title.text: Hooverville on waterfront of Seattle, Washington

content.text: An estimated two million Americans became homeless in the early years of the Great Depression. Many moved to temporary settlements on city outskirts, where they built basic shelters out of scrap wood, tin, and cardboard. Residents and the general public called these unauthorized encampments "Hoovervilles."

title.text: Roads closed into city by striking farmers

content.text: A group of farmers block a highway in South Dakota during the Farmers' Holiday Association strike of 1932. After unsuccessfully lobbying for farm aid and tariff reform to help them sell their crops overseas, frustrated Midwestern farmers withheld crops and disrupted shipments to demand higher prices and government aid.

title.text: Hunger marchers in Washington, D.C., 1931

content.text: Protesters in Washington, D.C., hold signs saying "Not a cent for war—all funds for the unemployed" and "Hoover's stagger plan [means] starvation." Hunger marches such as the one pictured here became a common form of protest as unemployed workers demanded food, jobs, and government aid.

contents.text: The economic crisis set the stage for the 1932 election between Republican Herbert Hoover, running for reelection, and Democrat Franklin D. Roosevelt.
Read excerpts from campaign speeches given by Herbert Hoover and Franklin D. Roosevelt. Then answer the question below.

content.text: The function of the federal government in these times is to use its…powers and its strength for the protection of citizens and local governments…against forces beyond their control. It is not the function of the government to relieve individuals of their responsibilities to their neighbors, or to relieve private institutions of their responsibilities to the public, or the local government to the states, or the responsibilities of state governments to the federal government.
It does not follow, because our difficulties are [extreme]…that we must turn to a [government-controlled] social or economic system in order to cure our troubles.…That is tyranny.

Our Republican leaders tell us economic laws…cause [economic] panics which no one could prevent. But while they [speak] of economic laws, men and women are starving.…If we get the chance, the federal government will assume bold leadership in distress relief.

Throughout the nation, men and women, forgotten in the political philosophy of the government of the last years look to us here for guidance and for more…opportunity.…I pledge you, I pledge myself, to a new deal for the American people.…This is more than a political campaign; it is a call to arms. Give me your help, not to win votes alone, but to win in this crusade to restore America to its people.

contents.text: The economic crisis set the stage for the 1932 election between Republican Herbert Hoover, running for reelection, and Democrat Franklin D. Roosevelt.
Read excerpts from campaign speeches given by Herbert Hoover and Franklin D. Roosevelt. Then answer the question below.

content.text: The function of the federal government in these times is to use its…powers and its strength for the protection of citizens and local governments…against forces beyond their control. It is not the function of the government to relieve individuals of their responsibilities to their neighbors, or to relieve private institutions of their responsibilities to the public, or the local government to the states, or the responsibilities of state governments to the federal government.
It does not follow, because our difficulties are [extreme]…that we must turn to a [government-controlled] social or economic system in order to cure our troubles.…That is tyranny.

Our Republican leaders tell us economic laws…cause [economic] panics which no one could prevent. But while they [speak] of economic laws, men and women are starving.…If we get the chance, the federal government will assume bold leadership in distress relief.

Throughout the nation, men and women, forgotten in the political philosophy of the government of the last years look to us here for guidance and for more…opportunity.…I pledge you, I pledge myself, to a new deal for the American people.…This is more than a political campaign; it is a call to arms. Give me your help, not to win votes alone, but to win in this crusade to restore America to its people.

contents.text: When the Great Depression began in 1929, Americans looked to President Herbert Hoover for leadership. He urged businesses to avoid cutting jobs, and he encouraged Americans to rely on local charity rather than federal assistance.

contents.text: The economic crisis set the stage for the 1932 election between Republican Herbert Hoover, running for reelection, and Democrat Franklin D. Roosevelt.
Read excerpts from campaign speeches given by Herbert Hoover and Franklin D. Roosevelt. Then answer the question below.

content.text: The function of the federal government in these times is to use its…powers and its strength for the protection of citizens and local governments…against forces beyond their control. It is not the function of the government to relieve individuals of their responsibilities to their neighbors, or to relieve private institutions of their responsibilities to the public, or the local government to the states, or the responsibilities of state governments to the federal government.
It does not follow, because our difficulties are [extreme]…that we must turn to a [government-controlled] social or economic system in order to cure our troubles.…That is tyranny.

Our Republican leaders tell us economic laws…cause [economic] panics which no one could prevent. But while they [speak] of economic laws, men and women are starving.…If we get the chance, the federal government will assume bold leadership in distress relief.

Throughout the nation, men and women, forgotten in the political philosophy of the government of the last years look to us here for guidance and for more…opportunity.…I pledge you, I pledge myself, to a new deal for the American people.…This is more than a political campaign; it is a call to arms. Give me your help, not to win votes alone, but to win in this crusade to restore America to its people.

contents.text: Franklin D. Roosevelt won the 1932 presidential election by a landslide on his promise of a "new deal for the American people." So Roosevelt's government programs to combat the Great Depression became known as the New Deal. In his first inaugural address, Roosevelt gave additional information about his New Deal agenda. Match each excerpt from his inaugural address to its meaning.

draggableItems.text: The agricultural economy can only be repaired by raising farmers' incomes and living standards.
The problems caused by the Great Depression can be solved as long as people don't panic.
To fix the country's enormous problems, the president may need to temporarily assume more power than is traditional.
The government can immediately reduce unemployment by hiring people to do important work for the country.

staticItems.text: Let me assert my firm belief that the only thing we have to fear is fear itself—nameless, unreasoning, unjustified terror which paralyzes needed efforts…

Our greatest primary task is to put people to work.…It can be accomplished in part by direct recruiting by the government…accomplishing greatly needed projects to stimulate and reorganize the use of our natural resources.

[We must] endeavor to provide a better use of the land.…The task [of recovery] can be helped by definite efforts to raise the values of agricultural products and with this [give farmers] the power to purchase the output of our cities.

It is to be hoped that the normal balance of executive and legislative authority may be wholly adequate to meet the unprecedented task before us. But it may be that an unprecedented demand and need for undelayed action may call for temporary departure from that normal balance of public procedure.

contents.text: Franklin D. Roosevelt won the 1932 presidential election by a landslide on his promise of a "new deal for the American people." So Roosevelt's government programs to combat the Great Depression became known as the New Deal. In his first inaugural address, Roosevelt made his famous declaration that "the only thing we have to fear is fear itself," and he gave additional information about his New Deal agenda. Read the excerpt from this address. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: Our greatest primary task is to put people to work.…It can be accomplished in part by direct recruiting by the government itself, treating the task as we would treat the emergency of a war, but at the same time, through this employment, accomplishing greatly needed projects to stimulate and reorganize the use of our natural resources.…

[We must] endeavor to provide a better use of the land.…The task can be helped by definite efforts to raise the values of agricultural products and with this the power to purchase the output of our cities [and] by preventing…the growing loss through foreclosure of our small homes and our farms.…

It is to be hoped that the normal balance of executive and legislative authority may be wholly adequate to meet the unprecedented task before us. But it may be that an unprecedented demand and need for undelayed action may call for temporary departure from that normal balance of public procedure.…In the event that the national emergency is still critical…I shall ask the Congress for…broad executive power to wage a war against the emergency.

contents.text: Many of the New Deal's most impactful programs were passed during the first one hundred days of the Roosevelt administration, between March and June of 1933. Since the New Deal, historians often measure a presidency's early success by its accomplishments in the "First Hundred Days."

One of the Great Depression's biggest crises was the failure of the banking industry. When President Roosevelt took office, one of his first goals was to restore public confidence in the banking system. Match each action related to the banking industry to its effect.

draggableItems.text: Because no one can withdraw money from banks, the government gains time to act.
Over the next week, Americans return over $1 billion to the banking system by depositing money into reopened banks.
Only banks that are found to be "financially sound" are given permission to reopen, while those with serious problems remain closed.
Without the funds to pay their customers, thousands of banks are forced to close.

staticItems.text: Before Roosevelt takes office, customers across the country attempt to withdraw more money than banks have available.
On his second day in office, Roosevelt declares a national bank holiday, ordering every bank in the country to shut down.
Congress passes the Emergency Banking Act, sending federal examiners to inspect the financial records of the closed banks.
Before banks reopen, Roosevelt delivers his first "fireside chat" radio address to explain why Americans should trust reopened banks.

contents.text: Franklin D. Roosevelt won the 1932 presidential election by a landslide on his promise of a "new deal for the American people." So Roosevelt's government programs to combat the Great Depression became known as the New Deal. In his first inaugural address, Roosevelt gave additional information about his New Deal agenda. Match each excerpt from his inaugural address to its meaning.

draggableItems.text: The problems caused by the Great Depression can be solved as long as people don't panic.
The government can immediately reduce unemployment by hiring people to do important work for the country.
To fix the country's enormous problems, the president may need to temporarily assume more power than is traditional.
The agricultural economy can only be repaired by raising farmers' incomes and living standards.

staticItems.text: Let me assert my firm belief that the only thing we have to fear is fear itself—nameless, unreasoning, unjustified terror which paralyzes needed efforts…

Our greatest primary task is to put people to work.…It can be accomplished in part by direct recruiting by the government…accomplishing greatly needed projects to stimulate and reorganize the use of our natural resources.

[We must] endeavor to provide a better use of the land.…The task [of recovery] can be helped by definite efforts to raise the values of agricultural products and with this [give farmers] the power to purchase the output of our cities.

It is to be hoped that the normal balance of executive and legislative authority may be wholly adequate to meet the unprecedented task before us. But it may be that an unprecedented demand and need for undelayed action may call for temporary departure from that normal balance of public procedure.

contents.text: Franklin D. Roosevelt won the 1932 presidential election by a landslide on his promise of a "new deal for the American people." So Roosevelt's government programs to combat the Great Depression became known as the New Deal. In his first inaugural address, Roosevelt made his famous declaration that "the only thing we have to fear is fear itself," and he gave additional information about his New Deal agenda. Read the excerpt from this address. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: Our greatest primary task is to put people to work.…It can be accomplished in part by direct recruiting by the government itself, treating the task as we would treat the emergency of a war, but at the same time, through this employment, accomplishing greatly needed projects to stimulate and reorganize the use of our natural resources.…

[We must] endeavor to provide a better use of the land.…The task can be helped by definite efforts to raise the values of agricultural products and with this the power to purchase the output of our cities [and] by preventing…the growing loss through foreclosure of our small homes and our farms.…

It is to be hoped that the normal balance of executive and legislative authority may be wholly adequate to meet the unprecedented task before us. But it may be that an unprecedented demand and need for undelayed action may call for temporary departure from that normal balance of public procedure.…In the event that the national emergency is still critical…I shall ask the Congress for…broad executive power to wage a war against the emergency.

contents.text: Many of the New Deal's most impactful programs were passed during the first one hundred days of the Roosevelt administration, between March and June of 1933. Since the New Deal, historians often measure a presidency's early success by its accomplishments in the "First Hundred Days."

One of the Great Depression's biggest crises was the failure of the banking industry. When President Roosevelt took office, one of his first goals was to restore public confidence in the banking system. Match each action related to the banking industry to its effect.

draggableItems.text: Only banks that are found to be "financially sound" are given permission to reopen, while those with serious problems remain closed.
Because no one can withdraw money from banks, the government gains time to act.
Without the funds to pay their customers, thousands of banks are forced to close.
Over the next week, Americans return over $1 billion to the banking system by depositing money into reopened banks.

staticItems.text: Before Roosevelt takes office, customers across the country attempt to withdraw more money than banks have available.
On his second day in office, Roosevelt declares a national bank holiday, ordering every bank in the country to shut down.
Congress passes the Emergency Banking Act, sending federal examiners to inspect the financial records of the closed banks.
Before banks reopen, Roosevelt delivers his first "fireside chat" radio address to explain why Americans should trust reopened banks.

pieces.text: The 1929 stock market crash revealed that consumers and banks had been making risky investments in stocks without knowing much about the companies they were investing in. To prevent a similar crisis in the future, the
required most companies selling stocks to

, meaning share, information about them and their financial performance. If companies were caught lying, customers could file lawsuits against them. So, the act enabled consumers to make more informed choices about their investments.
The

went even further. It created the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), an agency of the federal government with the power to enforce national laws about the sale of securities. contents.text: Franklin D. Roosevelt won the 1932 presidential election by a landslide on his promise of a "new deal for the American people." So Roosevelt's government programs to combat the Great Depression became known as the New Deal. In his first inaugural address, Roosevelt gave additional information about his New Deal agenda. Match each excerpt from his inaugural address to its meaning.

draggableItems.text: To fix the country's enormous problems, the president may need to temporarily assume more power than is traditional.
The problems caused by the Great Depression can be solved as long as people don't panic.
The agricultural economy can only be repaired by raising farmers' incomes and living standards.
The government can immediately reduce unemployment by hiring people to do important work for the country.

staticItems.text: Let me assert my firm belief that the only thing we have to fear is fear itself—nameless, unreasoning, unjustified terror which paralyzes needed efforts…

Our greatest primary task is to put people to work.…It can be accomplished in part by direct recruiting by the government…accomplishing greatly needed projects to stimulate and reorganize the use of our natural resources.

[We must] endeavor to provide a better use of the land.…The task [of recovery] can be helped by definite efforts to raise the values of agricultural products and with this [give farmers] the power to purchase the output of our cities.

It is to be hoped that the normal balance of executive and legislative authority may be wholly adequate to meet the unprecedented task before us. But it may be that an unprecedented demand and need for undelayed action may call for temporary departure from that normal balance of public procedure.

was President Franklin D. Roosevelt's attempt to solve the major economic problems created by the Great Depression of the 1930s. During his first term (1933–1937), President Roosevelt outlined three goals of his New Deal programs:

(1935–1938). Read the following excerpt from Roosevelt's speech. Then answer the question below.

pieces.text: New Deal programs were popular during President Roosevelt's first years in office, but the U.S. economy continued to struggle. So, in early 1935, President Roosevelt's State of the Union address to Congress launched what historians call the
(1935–1938). Read the following excerpt from Roosevelt's speech. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: [The] time has come for action by the national government. I shall send to [Congress], in a few days, definite recommendations…[that] will cover the broad subjects of unemployment insurance and old age insurance, of benefits for children, for others, for the handicapped, for maternity care and for other aspects of dependency and illness.…
[The] first practical steps can be made through the proposals which I shall suggest in relation to giving work to the unemployed.…

This new program of emergency public employment should…be useful—not just for a day, or a year, but useful in the sense that it affords permanent improvement in living conditions or that it creates future new wealth for the Nation.

contents.text: Look back at the excerpt. These choices are correct:

content.text: create new jobs for the unemployed to provide long-term economic security

explanationText.text: Roosevelt says the first steps of his plan involve "giving work to the unemployed." He also says the plan should provide "permanent" improvements, meaning congressional action to address long-term problems like finding employment.

content.text: provide long-term economic security through insurance programs

explanationText.text: Roosevelt shares plans for "unemployment insurance and old age insurance" to make sure citizens are protected financially if they lose their jobs or grow too old to work. Together, jobs and insurance programs were meant to provide lasting economic security.

contents.text: These choices are not correct:

content.text: focus on short-term cash relief instead of any need for longer-term national growth

explanationText.text: Roosevelt does not mention cash relief. He says the focus of the Second New Deal programs will be on providing insurance programs and long-term employment creating "future new wealth for the Nation."

content.text: reduce government involvement in the economy and let private businesses hire more people

explanationText.text: Roosevelt does not propose reducing government involvement. Instead, he proposes more government programs like insurance for the elderly and unemployed.

contents.text: With strong support from Congress, President Roosevelt easily gained support for his new plans. Lawmakers approved nearly $5 billion in new spending to launch the Second New Deal. Instead of just offering temporary relief, this massive wave of funding created programs focused on long-term stability, like providing electricity in remote areas and creating insurance programs for the elderly.

was President Franklin D. Roosevelt's attempt to solve the major economic problems created by the Great Depression of the 1930s. During his first term (1933–1937), President Roosevelt outlined three goals of his New Deal programs:
of the immediate economic suffering of the unemployed and poor through direct aid and temporary employment,
of the U.S. economy to normal, stable levels of employment and economic growth, and
of institutions and laws to prevent a similar economic crisis in the future.

contents.text: Decide which goal each New Deal activity best supported.

questions.text: The National Recovery Administration (NRA) set prices and wages in many industries to help the economy expand again.
The Home Owners' Loan Corporation (HOLC) helped struggling families keep their houses by providing immediate loans to help pay their home debt.
The Civil Works Administration (CWA) provided short-term manual-labor jobs to millions of unemployed Americans.
The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) set regulations to stop the risky, dishonest stock market practices that helped cause the Great Depression.

pieces.text: New Deal programs were popular during President Roosevelt's first years in office, but the U.S. economy continued to struggle. So, in early 1935, President Roosevelt's State of the Union address to Congress launched what historians call the
(1935–1938). Read the following excerpt from Roosevelt's speech. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: [The] time has come for action by the national government. I shall send to [Congress], in a few days, definite recommendations…[that] will cover the broad subjects of unemployment insurance and old age insurance, of benefits for children, for others, for the handicapped, for maternity care and for other aspects of dependency and illness.…
[The] first practical steps can be made through the proposals which I shall suggest in relation to giving work to the unemployed.…

This new program of emergency public employment should…be useful—not just for a day, or a year, but useful in the sense that it affords permanent improvement in living conditions or that it creates future new wealth for the Nation.

the government just relying on short-term relief. WPA workers focused exclusively on building and restoring federal government offices in Washington, D.C.
The WPA helped many people find jobs and earn enough money to feed their families during hard times.

contents.text: Look back at the sources. These choices are correct:

content.text: Workers built long-lasting infrastructure, such as roads, bridges, and airports, that improved their communities.

explanationText.text: The images show that WPA projects were located across the country and focused on developing long-lasting infrastructure like LaGuardia Airport in New York and Main Street in Evansville, Indiana. The first image caption says that WPA workers built over 40,000 new public buildings, including 1,000 libraries and 225 hospitals.

content.text: The WPA helped many people find jobs and earn enough money to feed their families during hard times.

explanationText.text: The description of projects says that the WPA employed over 8 million people. The letter from a WPA worker says the WPA is "the only thing that is keeping my family from starving."

contents.text: These choices are not correct:

content.text: The WPA built lasting partnerships with private industries that hired unemployed workers.

pieces.text: The description of projects says the WPA spent around $11 billion to put over 8 million people directly on the federal payroll. The letter from a WPA worker says that he
get a job in a private industry.

content.text: WPA workers focused exclusively on building and restoring federal government offices in Washington, D.C.

explanationText.text: The images show that WPA projects were located across the country. It also shows that WPA workers not only constructed buildings but built other forms of infrastructure, such as airports, roads, and tourist areas.

On March 12, 1933, eight days after taking office, President Roosevelt delivered the first of his fireside chats. The topic of this speech was the

. In response to bank failures caused by the Great Depression, Roosevelt had declared a national "bank holiday." During this period, all U.S. banks were closed for four days to prevent people from withdrawing their money. When too many people withdraw their money at once, banks can fail. After the holiday, banks deemed safe were allowed to reopen.

contents.text: Read the following excerpt. You can use the audio button to hear a recording of Roosevelt's radio address. Then answer the question below.

paragraphs.text: My friends, I want to talk for a few minutes with the people of the United States about banking—to talk with the comparatively few who understand the mechanics of banking, but more particularly with the overwhelming majority of you who use banks for the making of deposits and the drawing of checks. I want to tell you what has been done in the last few days, and why it was done, and what the next steps are going to be.

pieces.text: I recognize that the many proclamations from state capitols and from Washington, the legislation, the Treasury regulations, and so forth,
for the most part in banking and legal terms, ought to be explained for the benefit of the average citizen. I owe this in particular because of the

with which everybody has accepted the inconvenience and the hardships of the banking holiday. And I know that when you understand what we in Washington have been about, I shall continue to have your cooperation as fully as I have had your sympathy and your help during the past week.

pieces.text: On May 7, 1933, Roosevelt gave a fireside chat about his

. The New Deal was a set of programs to help provide immediate aid to those suffering from the Great Depression, bring the economy back to normal levels of growth, and reform economic institutions to prevent a similar crisis in the future.

contents.text: Read and listen to the following excerpt from Roosevelt's chat about the New Deal. Then answer the question below.

pieces.text: Two months ago, as you know, we were facing serious problems. The country was dying by inches. It was dying because trade and commerce had declined to dangerously low levels.…There were just two alternatives at that time. The first was to allow the
to continue, credit to be withheld, money to go into hiding, thus forcing liquidation and bankruptcy of banks, and railroads, and insurance companies and a

content.text: recapitalizing of all business and all property on a lower level

pieces.text: .… A prompt program applied as quickly as possible seemed to me not only justified, but imperative to our national security.

paragraphs.text: The Congress—and when I say the Congress I mean the members of both political parties—fully understood this and gave me generous and intelligent support. The members of the Congress realized that the methods of normal times had to be replaced in the emergency by measures that were suited to the serious and pressing requirements of the moment. On March 12, 1933, eight days after taking office, President Roosevelt delivered the first of his fireside chats. The topic of this speech was the

. In response to bank failures caused by the Great Depression, Roosevelt had declared a national "bank holiday." During this period, all U.S. banks were closed for four days to prevent people from withdrawing their money. When too many people withdraw their money at once, banks can fail. After the holiday, banks deemed safe were allowed to reopen.

contents.text: Read and listen to the following excerpt. Then answer the question below.

paragraphs.text: My friends, I want to talk for a few minutes with the people of the United States about banking—to talk with the comparatively few who understand the mechanics of banking, but more particularly with the overwhelming majority of you who use banks for the making of deposits and the drawing of checks. I want to tell you what has been done in the last few days, and why it was done, and what the next steps are going to be.

pieces.text: I recognize that the many proclamations from state capitols and from Washington, the legislation, the Treasury regulations, and so forth,
for the most part in banking and legal terms, ought to be explained for the benefit of the average citizen. I owe this in particular because of the

with which everybody has accepted the inconvenience and the hardships of the banking holiday. And I know that when you understand what we in Washington have been about, I shall continue to have your cooperation as fully as I have had your sympathy and your help during the past week.

On March 12, 1933, eight days after taking office, President Roosevelt delivered the first of his fireside chats. The topic of this speech was the

. In response to bank failures caused by the Great Depression, Roosevelt had declared a national "bank holiday." During this period, all U.S. banks were closed for four days to prevent people from withdrawing their money. When too many people withdraw their money at once, banks can fail. After the holiday, banks deemed safe were allowed to reopen.

contents.text: Read the following excerpt. You can use the audio button to hear a recording of Roosevelt's radio address. Then answer the question below.

paragraphs.text: My friends, I want to talk for a few minutes with the people of the United States about banking—to talk with the comparatively few who understand the mechanics of banking, but more particularly with the overwhelming majority of you who use banks for the making of deposits and the drawing of checks. I want to tell you what has been done in the last few days, and why it was done, and what the next steps are going to be.

pieces.text: I recognize that the many proclamations from state capitols and from Washington, the legislation, the Treasury regulations, and so forth,
for the most part in banking and legal terms, ought to be explained for the benefit of the average citizen. I owe this in particular because of the

with which everybody has accepted the inconvenience and the hardships of the banking holiday. And I know that when you understand what we in Washington have been about, I shall continue to have your cooperation as fully as I have had your sympathy and your help during the past week.

content.text: The banking crisis was caused by a small number of banks, and most banks didn't do anything wrong.

explanationText.text: Roosevelt says that some bankers were "dishonest in their handling of the people's funds." But he says that this was "not true in the vast majority of our banks."

content.text: The federal government is getting involved to determine which banks are trustworthy.

explanationText.text: Roosevelt also says that it is "the government's job to straighten out this situation," meaning determine which banks were trustworthy and which were not, and that "that job is being performed."

contents.text: These choices are not correct:

content.text: The problems caused by the banking crisis will resolve themselves on their own if people are patient.

explanationText.text: Roosevelt does not say that the banking crisis will solve itself. Instead, he says that the government had the responsibility to solve the problem.

content.text: Consumers are to blame for the banking crisis because they needlessly panicked about the safety of their money.

explanationText.text: Roosevelt says that Americans could not differentiate between safe and unsafe banks, and so they withdrew their money. But he does not blame them for the banking crisis, and instead blames the banks who were risky with deposits.

The members of the Congress realized that the methods of normal times had to be replaced in the emergency by measures that were suited to the serious and pressing requirements of the moment. The function of Congress is to decide what has to be done and to select the appropriate agency to carry out its will. That policy it has strictly adhered to. The only thing that has been happening has been to designate the president of the United States as the agency to carry out certain of the purposes of the Congress. This was constitutional, and is constitutional, and it is in keeping with the past American tradition.

content.text: The New Deal is the only reasonable response to the Great Depression, because the only alternative is doing nothing about people's suffering.

explanationText.text: Roosevelt says that the two responses to the Great Depression are to let the economy spiral, or to have "a prompt program applied as quickly as possible," which means Roosevelt's New Deal program.

content.text: People should not be afraid of a strong presidency, because Roosevelt's actions are in line with the American constitutional tradition.

explanationText.text: In the second paragraph, Roosevelt reiterates that Congress gave the president authority to act, and that doing this "was constitutional, and is constitutional, and it is in keeping with the past American tradition."

contents.text: These choices are not correct:

content.text: Because Congress is unwilling to act to solve the problem, Americans should be willing to give wider powers to the president.

explanationText.text: In the second paragraph, Roosevelt emphasizes that Congress recognizes the crisis and has constitutionally fulfilled their duties to make laws. He does not say that the president should have more power.

content.text: Americans must recognize that the Constitution has to be amended to allow the federal government to end the Great Depression.

explanationText.text: Roosevelt says that Congress recognizes that "the methods of normal times had to be replaced in the emergency," but he does not say anything about constitutional amendments. In fact, he emphasizes that the New Deal programs are constitutional.

contents.text: Read and listen to the following excerpt from Roosevelt's fireside chat about New Deal legislation. Then answer the question below.

paragraphs.text: To you, the people of this country, all of us in Washington, the members of the Congress and the members of this administration, owe a profound debt of gratitude. Throughout the Depression you have been patient. You have granted us wide powers. You have encouraged us with a widespread approval of our purposes. Every ounce of strength, every resource at our command, we have devoted and we are devoted to the end of justifying your confidence. We are encouraged to believe that a wise and sensible beginning has been made. In the present spirit of mutual confidence and the present spirit of mutual encouragement, we go forward.

By claiming that the government owes Americans "a profound debt of gratitude," he clarifies that individual Americans are the only ones who can end the Depression.
By stating "you have granted us wide powers," he reiterates that the American people voted him into office to take action.

On March 12, 1933, eight days after taking office, President Roosevelt delivered the first of his fireside chats. The topic of this speech was the

. In response to bank failures caused by the Great Depression, Roosevelt had declared a national "bank holiday." During this period, all U.S. banks were closed for four days to prevent people from withdrawing their money. When too many people withdraw their money at once, banks can fail. After the holiday, banks deemed safe were allowed to reopen.

contents.text: Read and listen to the following excerpt. Then answer the question below.

paragraphs.text: My friends, I want to talk for a few minutes with the people of the United States about banking—to talk with the comparatively few who understand the mechanics of banking, but more particularly with the overwhelming majority of you who use banks for the making of deposits and the drawing of checks. I want to tell you what has been done in the last few days, and why it was done, and what the next steps are going to be.

pieces.text: I recognize that the many proclamations from state capitols and from Washington, the legislation, the Treasury regulations, and so forth,
for the most part in banking and legal terms, ought to be explained for the benefit of the average citizen. I owe this in particular because of the

with which everybody has accepted the inconvenience and the hardships of the banking holiday. And I know that when you understand what we in Washington have been about, I shall continue to have your cooperation as fully as I have had your sympathy and your help during the past week.

paragraphs.text: The Congress—and when I say the Congress I mean the members of both political parties—fully understood this and gave me generous and intelligent support. The members of the Congress realized that the methods of normal times had to be replaced in the emergency by measures that were suited to the serious and pressing requirements of the moment. There was no actual surrender of power; Congress still retained its constitutional authority, to legislate and to appropriate, and no one has the slightest desire to change the balance of these powers. The function of Congress is to decide what has to be done and to select the appropriate agency to carry out its will. That policy it has strictly adhered to. The only thing that has been happening has been to designate the president of the United States as the agency to carry out certain of the purposes of the Congress. This was constitutional, and is constitutional, and it is in keeping with the past American tradition.

contents.text: Look back at the excerpt. This choice is correct:

content.text: Strong action by Congress and the president is constitutional, and it is necessary to prevent people's suffering.

explanationText.text: Roosevelt says that the two responses to the Great Depression are to let the economy spiral, or to have "a prompt program applied as quickly as possible," which means Roosevelt's New Deal program. Roosevelt also says that Congress gave the president authority to act, and that doing this "was constitutional, and is constitutional, and it is in keeping with the past American tradition."

contents.text: These choices are not correct:

content.text: The Constitution does not allow the government to respond enough to the Depression, and so it should be amended.

explanationText.text: Roosevelt says that Congress recognizes that "the methods of normal times had to be replaced in the emergency," but he does not say anything about constitutional amendments. In fact, he emphasizes that the New Deal programs are constitutional.

content.text: The president, not Congress, must be given additional powers by voters in order to create programs to fight the Depression.

explanationText.text: In the second paragraph, Roosevelt emphasizes that Congress recognizes the crisis and has constitutionally fulfilled their duties to make laws. He does not say that the president should have more power.

contents.text: Read and listen to the following excerpt from Roosevelt's fireside chat about New Deal legislation. Then answer the question below.

paragraphs.text: To you, the people of this country, all of us in Washington, the members of the Congress and the members of this administration, owe a profound debt of gratitude. Throughout the Depression you have been patient. You have granted us wide powers. You have encouraged us with a widespread approval of our purposes. Every ounce of strength, every resource at our command, we have devoted and we are devoted to the end of justifying your confidence. We are encouraged to believe that a wise and sensible beginning has been made. In the present spirit of mutual confidence and the present spirit of mutual encouragement, we go forward.

content.text: to emphasize the close relationship he envisions between the American people and his presidency

explanationText.text: Mutual means something that two groups have in common. Roosevelt is saying that both the government and the American people trust each other and are working together to end the Depression. This reinforces a close relationship between his presidency and voters.

contents.text: The other choices are not correct:

content.text: to reiterate that people should not expect extreme measures to deal with the economic crisis

explanationText.text: Roosevelt actually says that the American people have granted the government "wide powers" to deal with the crisis.

content.text: to clarify that individual Americans are the only ones who can end the Great Depression

explanationText.text: Roosevelt thanks Americans for the patience while the government enacts programs to solve the crisis. He does not say that Americans' individual actions have helped with the Depression.
